messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] mcmcplots
messages.body_plain:
Wow, this is great.  Here are some quick thoughts:

1.  We should probably make a clear list (or maybe Bob has this list already) of the sorts of plots we want.  Roughly it goes something like this:

a.  The default (what we want as output of plot(...) of a stan object):  something that looks sort of like the right half of the current R2Winbugs plot, showing inferences for all 4 chains of all the saved quantities, using a sensible grouping so that vector and array parameters are clearly visible.

b.  Traceplots (by default inluding warmup iterations) for all the quantites saved or for any specified quantites, using diffferent colors for the different chains.

c.  Diagnostic plots such as what we've been talking about with Mike B., for example plots of avg acceptance probability vs. log density, plots of #leapfrog steps vs log density, etc.

d.  Other things that don't interest me, particularly, but other people like, things like density plots and caterpillar plots.

e.  Maybe there are some other graphs I'm forgetting?

2.  I have no problem with coda etc. but my impression is that the hard part right now is making the graphs.  The actual computation (R-hat, effective sample size, etc) is easy enough that I'd just as soon do it from scratch rather than invoke a dependence on another package that might get changed at some point.

3.  I love the idea of "outsiders" such as Ilya and McKay getting involved.  It might be that my most useful contribution at this point would be to explain clearly what I'm looking for, and why.  (Just as a starting point, one reason I like the crisp overview plots mentioned in 1a above is that this should allow us to see lots of parameters at once.  Traceplots, density plots, etc., are bulky.  My experience is that when there are dozens of pages of graphs, it's hard to get a picture of whats happening.  I much prefer a compact plot that shows _everything_ (or nearly everything), then the user can drill down and look at specific parameters as necessary.

What do you think?

See you
Andrew

On Jun 30, 2012, at 6:04 PM, Ilya Goldin wrote:

> Bob, thanks for the quick response. The replies below are all personal opinion; I do not speak for McKay, the primary creator and developer of mcmcplots (I believe he's waiting for membership approval to stan-dev).
>
> On Saturday, June 30, 2012, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > On a practical note, Stan is BSD licensed and we're trying
> > to do as many calculations on the output in C++ as possible
> > to make it easy to port to R, Matlab and Python (and Stata).
> > Because R is GPL-ed, the R glue code has to be GPL.
>
> Personally, I like BSD just fine, but some mcmcplots code is derived from GPL code (e.g., the coda package), and could not be relicensed without rewriting.
>
> > Multi-HTML output is a great idea.  I was just complaining
> > about how long full PDFs take to load of things like
> > traceplots.  (They print much better due to the vector
> > graphics, but are a pain for simple diagnostics.)
>
> HTML-and-PNG output is handy for diagnostics. An example is in beta-gamma-rho.zip, which I got via
>
> mcmcplot(mymcmc, c("beta", "gamma", "rho"), random=5)
>
> For publication, you wouldn't publish all plots of all parameters anyway, so to get vector graphics you might do
>
> pdf("caterpillar-delta.pdf")
> caterplot(mymcmc, "delta")
> dev.off()
>
> > I like your multiple-chain density plots.  I have no experience
> > interpreting them, though -- I don't know how stable to
> > expect the estimated densities to be.   Point estimates of
> > 95% intervals are going to be fairly high variance with our
> > default option of 1000 samples/chain.
> > How do you set up the density estimation parameters?
>
> This simply uses the R density() function. It would be reasonable to parametrize mcmcplots to use any a custom density calculation.
>
> > What's partial autocorrelation?
>
> McKay can give a better answer, but generally, http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_autocorrelation_function
>
> > Given that you have two chains, why is there only one
> > autocorrelation plot?  We'll have four chains by default.
>
> Right now, it displays just one chain; the default is to use the first chain. I can imagine a single plot that displays all chains, differentiating by color just as the other plots do.
>
> > We're particularly concerned about calculating effective
> > sample size and potential scale reduction (R-hat).
>
> If I'm not mistaken, R-hat is shown on the autocorrelation plot as the height of the dark grey rectangle (vs. the light grey background).
>
> > I think you could get better scale on the autocorrelation
> > graph by removing the 0 entry (it's always 1.0).
>
> Unconventional, but interesting. I wonder what Andrew has to say.
>
> > I'd rather have titles match the names of variables in
> > the plot verbatim rather than try to convert to greek.
>
> This is optional, and off by default, as in the enclosed beta-gamma-rho.zip.
>
> > Do you handle discrete parameters?  Stan doesn't do discrete
> > sampling (yet), but the output from R2WinBUGS (I don't know if
> > this is from coda) never made sense for discrete parameters.
>
> Great question! McKay?
>
> > We want to include something like a caterpillar plot for
> > multiple chains with 80% intervals and medians.  We're fussing
> > with scales here -- for instance, if we have something like
> > the typical regression parameters case, do we put them all on
> > the same scale or not?  We don't want to go so far as R2WinBUGS
> > and put everything on the same scale (as they do in their left-hand
> > plot).
>
> Caterpillars are already there, a sample is enclosed. See ?caterplot for more details, but in short, you can call caterplot(..., quantiles), where quantiles is a "list with two elements outer and inner. The outer element of the list should contain the quantiles of the posterior draws that will be plotted as the longer, thinner line. The inner element of the list should contain the quantiles of posterior draws that will be plotted as the shorter, thicker line. If missing, the default is to use list(outer=c(0.025,0.975),inner=c(0.16,0.84)), which corresponds to 95% and 68% credible intervals." By default, all parallel chains are collapsed into one chain before plotting.
>
> The typical regression parameters case is misleading. You might want all intercepts on the same scale, but you probably wouldn't want all slopes on the same scale, unless you conscientiously centered and rescaled all covariates. A trick you might use here is to use different parameter names to group parameters by their scale, so all beta parameters get their own scale, all gamma parameters get their own, etc., and these would be displayed on separate plots.
>
> Best,
> Ilya
>
>
> --
> -- Ilya Goldin <www.pitt.edu/~goldin <http://www.pitt.edu/~goldin>>

> <caterpillar-delta.pdf><beta-gamma-rho.zip>

Hi Bob,

Ilya has already given answers to many of your questions, so I just have a few comments below...

On Saturday, June 30, 2012 12:14:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks for the note.  We're about to announce
> an official 1.0 release of Stan.  We were just about to
> release when we figured out how to improve the auto-dif
> performance for densities without too much work, so we've
> been pushing those changes through.
>
> We're always happy to borrow others' code instead of
> writing it ourselves.
>
> On a practical note, Stan is BSD licensed and we're trying
> to do as many calculations on the output in C++ as possible
> to make it easy to port to R, Matlab and Python (and Stata).
> Because R is GPL-ed, the R glue code has to be GPL.
>
> Multi-HTML output is a great idea.  I was just complaining
> about how long full PDFs take to load of things like
> traceplots.  (They print much better due to the vector
> graphics, but are a pain for simple diagnostics.)
>
> I like your multiple-chain density plots.  I have no experience
> interpreting them, though -- I don't know how stable to
> expect the estimated densities to be.   Point estimates of
> 95% intervals are going to be fairly high variance with our
> default option of 1000 samples/chain.
>
> How do you set up the density estimation parameters?
>
> What's partial autocorrelation?

This is something that I've seen others talk about when monitoring MCMC convergence, so I included it in some of the plots (even though I don't find it particularly useful).  I just call the acf/pacf functions in stats to create the autocorrelation plots.  The dark grey areas on the plots are confidence intervals (as, for example, are produced in the "plot.acf" function).

>
> Given that you have two chains, why is there only one
> autocorrelation plot?  We'll have four chains by default.

I couldn't think of a way to display them all on the same plot without the plot feeling cluttered so I just chose to plot the first chain.

>
> We're particularly concerned about calculating effective
> sample size and potential scale reduction (R-hat).

Currently, ESS and Rhat values aren't incorporated into any plots in the mcmcplots package.  It would be good to incorporate these values into a plot, however.

>
> I think you could get better scale on the autocorrelation
> graph by removing the 0 entry (it's always 1.0).
>

This is a good point.  Thanks!

> I'd rather have titles match the names of variables in
> the plot verbatim rather than try to convert to greek.
>
> Do you handle discrete parameters?  Stan doesn't do discrete
> sampling (yet), but the output from R2WinBUGS (I don't know if
> this is from coda) never made sense for discrete parameters.

The package currently doesn't handle discrete parameters, but this is another good idea to think about implementing in the future.

>
> We want to include something like a caterpillar plot for
> multiple chains with 80% intervals and medians.  We're fussing
> with scales here -- for instance, if we have something like
> the typical regression parameters case, do we put them all on
> the same scale or not?  We don't want to go so far as R2WinBUGS
> and put everything on the same scale (as they do in their left-hand
> plot).

Ilya's idea of putting all parameters in a parameter "group" on the same scale might work nicely.  One of the motivations for writing the mcmcplots package was to create functions that made it easy to access different groups of parameters.  The package currently has the function "parms2plot" that tries to be smart about detecting which parameters form a group and which do not.  It could be relatively straightforward to implement a caterpillar plot that produces different scales for different parameter groups.

Ilya also noted that the caterplot function has the "quantiles" option to change the length of the intervals.  I also thought the density strips developed in Jackson (2008, "Displaying uncertainty with shading." The American Statistician, 62(4):340-347) were pretty slick, so I implemented density strips in the caterplot function with the "denstrip" option (which calls Jackson's own function and package).  The default is not to use density strips, because I don't think they are widely used (but I like them, anyway).

>
> - Bob
>
>
> On 6/30/12 10:13 AM, Ilya Goldin wrote:
> > Dear Stan crew,
> >
> > Congratulations on your work on Stan. We're very excited about what it means for the future of Bayesian modeling.
> >
> > We see that you've been working on your own graphing code for MCMC output. We have an R package, mcmcplots, that may be
> > relevant at this stage.
> >
> > mcmcplots has some pretty useful MCMC graphing functionality, including plots of chain trace, density, autocorrelation,
> > and caterpillar plots. It's fast, and has a host of neat features. For instance, given an object of multiple chains of
> > multiple parameters, it can save PNG images for each parameter and collate the images into an HTML file with a table of
> > contents. This makes for a fast visual way of sanity-checking the output of a complex run.
> >
> > Attached is a screenshot of one of the mcmcplots outputs. This is a combination of trace, density, and autocorrelation
> > into a single image. The vertical bars on the density indicate 95% CIs for each of two chains, red and blue. The plot is
> > of a parameter delta[1], and the plot title is displayed using the greek letter delta.
> >
> > The code is here: https://github.com/s-mckay-curtis/mcmcplots <https://github.com/s-mckay-curtis/mcmcplots> . You're
> > welcome to simply use the code on open source terms, of course, but we'd also be happy to work with you to add the
> > functionality you need to mcmcplots. Please let us know if you'd be interested in working with us so mcmcplots can grow
> > to suit Stan.
> >
> > P.S. If you'd like to kick the tires, please use the code from github. A new release including some bug fixes is
> > imminent, but has not yet happened.
> >
> > Best regards,
> > S. McKay Curtis and Ilya Goldin

Jiqiang

messages.subject: collaborating on RStan
messages.body_plain:
(Affix project manager hat.)  How are we going
to organize responsibility for RStan?

Daniel and I are in the best position to deal with
coding the mcmc::chains object (what Andrew calls
the "Stan object").

Jiqiang's leading the RStan effort and has the
infrastructure for generating the data for all the plots
we care about in place (other than perhaps smallest
posterior intervals, for which we're going to use
the R package due to the complexity of the estimator).
The complexity is mainly the integration with C++
(which is compounded by the compiled nature of Stan's models).

Ilya's proposing we treat the mcmcplots package as being
a source of MCMC graphics and that we integrate at
the level of RStan calling mcmcplots through R.
Pro:  This is the cleanest break as it means we won't
be collaborating on code in the same repository.  Cons:  It
adds a dependency to RStan we have to keep up with.

Answers to other questions are inlined below.

On 7/1/12 8:43 AM, Ilya Goldin wrote:
> On Sunday, July 1, 2012, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>
>     Wow, this is great.  Here are some quick thoughts:
>
>     1.  We should probably make a clear list (or maybe Bob has this list already) of the sorts of plots we want.

We've sort of been making it up as we go along.

The closest we have to a spec of work is the
top-level TO-DO list.  Some of this we're playing
by ear after seeing how it looks.

We're talking about a bunch of different things
for RStan here:

-3.  Translating a Stan model to C++

-2.  Compiling the C++ Model

-1.  Invoking the C++ model with data from R.

-0.5.  Getting data back into C++ with an object
view wrapper in R.

0.  Printing
As Jiqiang already has it -- like R2WinBUGS.
Columns w/o too many sig figs for mean, median,
sd, quantiles, R-hat, and ESS.

+ smallest posterior intervals?

1.  Plots Andrew Wants (aka Version 1 Priorities)

We don't have exact design specs for this, just
previous examples.

A.  Everything in one plot
This is the one like the right side of the R2WinBUGs
plot.  We want to see at a glance the R-hat status,
medians and quantiles for all the variables (or some
of each of them for large multivariate params).  Right now
we're considering a horizontal layout like the left
side of R2WinBUGS, but with different scales per
multivariate parameter and problematic R-hat illustrated
with shading.

Modulo the sorting and fixed scale, this looks like it
fits the Wikipedia description of "caterpillar plot".

B.  Traceplots
Traceplots for each variable, potentially with quantile
and median bars w. warmup highlighted in a different color.

C.  Diagnostic Plots
Given that Stan's adaptive and can have varying step sizes
and numbers of steps per iteration, plotting these for
accepted and rejected proposals.  No plans on how to do that yet.
We could follow Coda and treat duplicate param vectors as
rejections.

2. Other plots

C.  Densities / Histograms
Across chains or combined chains (or both)

D.  Autocorrelations

>
>     2.  I have no problem with coda etc. but my impression is that the hard part right now is making the graphs.

That's only a small part of it.  The hard part's
getting R and C++ communicating across all the platforms
required for submission to CRAN.

 >     The
>     actual computation (R-hat, effective sample size, etc) is easy enough that I'd just as soon do it from scratch
>     rather than invoke a dependence on another package that might get changed at some point.
>
>
> True. The killer thing is that the stan object needs to have sensible accessor methods!

No problem -- Daniel and I can add
whatever's necessary to the mcmc::chains object.

I think the plan's still to do smallest posterior
intervals with the R package.

>     3.  I love the idea of "outsiders" such as Ilya and McKay getting involved.  ...

This is one of the big selling points for open-source tools.

I like to think of it as allowing an open notion of "insider".

>We need to
>
> a) determine the list of plots that you want for stan

See above for the essentials for version 1.

> b) find a way of extracting everything that's necessary for the plots out of the stan object or auxillary functions

One issue we're concerned about is scalability.

If whole chain data needs to be read into an R object to
compute statistics (as opposed to just displaying the
results), it's going to be slow and memory
intensive.

Reading data one parameter at a time's no big deal assuming
R can garbage collect.  We'll have to do this for smallest
posterior intervals anyway.

On the other hand, data in R makes it much easier
to serialize -- we don't know how to serialize our C++
object for R (it's not a C++ issue -- I could serialize
the object if I knew the hooks and protocolos).

> c) document how to invoke mcmcplots functions, possibly with some changes from defaults, to follow the visualization
> procedure that you recommend

I don't think we need any separate doc beyond
the mcmcplots doc.

If RStan calls mcmcplots, the calling pattern will
be in the code and we can just doc what's confusing there
when we get to it.

- Bob

For anything per chain like this I think it's important to
see all the chains. You could put them all on one plot with
different colored bars.

In most cases, I think we'd expect them to be roughly the
same in all chains, so this'd give you a way to compare them.

>     We're particularly concerned about calculating effective
>     sample size and potential scale reduction (R-hat).
>
>
> Currently, ESS and Rhat values aren't incorporated into any plots in the mcmcplots package. It would be good to
> incorporate these values into a plot, however.

We were mainly thinking about using them
to color code other plots.  They're just
single values per parameter (not per chain,
though you could calculate ESS per chain).

>     We want to include something like a caterpillar plot for
>     multiple chains with 80% intervals and medians. We're fussing

>     plot).
>
>

The only thing we've been concerned about for that
approach is when the parameter group isn't well scaled,
like many vectors of regression coefficients (cue Andrew to
say it's the user's job to normalize the data [this will
at least partly mitigate the worst cases]).

> One of the motivations
> for writing the mcmcplots package was to create functions that made it easy to access different groups of parameters.
> The package currently has the function "parms2plot" that tries to be smart about detecting which parameters form a group
> and which do not. It could be relatively straightforward to implement a caterpillar plot that produces different scales
> for different parameter groups.

That's exactly what we've been thinking about.

The "groups" in question for us are just the
multivarate parameters.  These will get the same
name, but the translation back and forth of
the multivariate parameters is a pain (though I think
we all (or at least most) of the infrastructure we need.

> Ilya also noted that the caterplot function has the "quantiles" option to change the length of the intervals. I also

> approach is when the parameter group isn't well scaled,
> like many vectors of regression coefficients (cue Andrew to
> say it's the user's job to normalize the data [this will

I'm not so worried about this.  If the parameters in a vector are clearly on different scales, the user can just display them individually (this should be doable using some argument to the function call).  The quick default display is intended to show (almost) everything in one place; the user can always zoom in as needed.

What I'm saying is, we want good defaults but, in doing so, I think it makes sense to make compactness a priority.  Using a common scale for a vector or array parameter allows the display to be cleaner.  I _don't_ want to go the way Bugs goes and treat each scalar like a completely separate parameter.

messages.body_plain:
It occurs to me that I didn't formally introduce myself other than "I tinker with mcmcplots". My apologies. I'm a postdoc at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon. My research looks at how people learn with different kinds of feedback in different learning contexts, including in intelligent tutoring systems and in computer-supported peer review in education. Practically speaking, I do a little bit of Bayesian modeling and still have much to learn. My work is very empirically oriented, and I like thinking about data visualization. My start with Bayesian modeling was under WinBUGS, with help from Howard Seltman (CMU) back in 2010. My dissertation would not have happened without the Gelman & Hill book. (Andrew, I think we emailed about minor errata at some point.) I try to contribute to mcmcplots as a way of giving back to the Bayesian modeling world without being a statistician.

It feels like we're arriving at a shared understanding of what mcmcplots needs to be able to do to serve as a visualization complement for Stan. It also seems imprudent to hold up the 1.0 release of Stan while the visualization stuff gets worked out.

My proposal is this. For Stan 1.0, we would release an accompanying mcmcplots (call it mcmcplots v. 0.5, since 0.4 is essentially ready) that provides the same outputs that mcmcplots already can but with the stan object as input. This seems feasible in the short term, and provides a reasonably useful subset of the wanted functionality (including density, trace plots, autocorrelation, and caterpillars). It will also serve as a test case for how we can work together.

In later mcmcplots releases, we will change some plots and add additional ones, which will ideally benefit both Stan and the other MCMC engines that mcmcplots already handles. We should keep a running desiderata for future mcmcplots releases (perhaps as a wiki or bug tracker). This is a long and interesting list, to be clarified and prioritized in the future.

a. Similar to R2WinBUGS, something like the right half of Figure C.2 here:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/bugsR/software.pdf

(This plot is basically a vertical caterpillar with 80% CI. In figure C.2 above, the chains are collapsed, but we would make this collapsing optional so that it's possible to juxtapose the 4 chains.)

b. Diagnostic plots, for example plots of avg acceptance probability vs. log density, plots of #leapfrog steps vs log density, etc.

c. On the overview plot for each parameter, a visual display of R-hat and/or n.eff. This could use visual cues to flag parameters with problematic R-hat or n.eff values, based on some threshold.

d. The autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation plots could get omitted from the parameter overview by default.

e. The autocorrelation plot could omit lag at 0.

f. The autocorrelation plot could optionally separate chains instead of collapsing them as it does now.

g. The autocorrelation plot could automatically flag the case of chains having very different autocorrelation. Is there a test for this?

h. It would be interesting to add somewhat more intelligent default visualization behavior. For instance, if any parameters have problematic R-hat / n.eff, diagnostic plots would by default get generated for these, but not for other parameters.

i. Pluggable density function for the density plots.

j. Automatically choose decent density functions depending on the parameter type. I remember hearing that some density functions are especially appropriate for MCMC simulations.

k. Somehow handle discrete parameters, once Stan does.

--
-- Ilya Goldin <www.pitt.edu/~goldin <http://www.pitt.edu/~goldin>>

> be collaborating on code in the same repository.  Cons:  It
> adds a dependency to RStan we have to keep up with.

Rather than RStan calling mcmcplots, I'd rather the user call mcmcplots, passing an mcmc::chains object, e.g.,

denplot(stanobj, "delta")

It would be nice to have a plot.stanobj function that displays a default overview, but optional.

> 1.  Plots Andrew Wants (aka Version 1 Priorities)

As per my message a minute ago, does it seem reasonable to have the Version 1 "spec" be simply consuming the Stan object and generating the same plots that mcmcplots already has, rather than tinkering with graphics?

> This is the one like the right side of the R2WinBUGs
> plot.  We want to see at a glance the R-hat status,
> medians and quantiles for all the variables (or some

> we're considering a horizontal layout like the left

> multivariate parameter and problematic R-hat illustrated
> with shading.
>
> Modulo the sorting and fixed scale, this looks like it
> fits the Wikipedia description of "caterpillar plot".

We're very close to this now. The caterpillar plot is there, you can customize the quantiles, you can uncollapse the chains, and you can generate a caterpillar plot for each parameter group. A reasonable scale is chosen automatically for each param group. The only missing item is R-hat.

> B.  Traceplots

> and median bars w. warmup highlighted in a different color.

Traceplots are there now, but without quantile bars or warm-up highlighting. Is warm-up in Stan like adaptation in JAGS?

> and numbers of steps per iteration, plotting these for
> accepted and rejected proposals.  No plans on how to do that yet.
> We could follow Coda and treat duplicate param vectors as
> rejections.

mcmcplots doesn't have this now. This is very interesting to me and I'd love to think about this, but perhaps this is not mandatory for v.1?

> C.  Densities / Histograms
> Across chains or combined chains (or both)

Already there.

> D.  Autocorrelations

Already there.

> One issue we're concerned about is scalability.
>
> If whole chain data needs to be read into an R object to
> compute statistics (as opposed to just displaying the
> results), it's going to be slow and memory
> intensive.

True, but rjags does this for JAGS now, and it seems reasonable to want access to whole chains on the R side for various summary statistics anyway. We could use this straightforward approach for v.1, and optimize later.

Best,
Ilya

--
-- Ilya Goldin <www.pitt.edu/~goldin <http://www.pitt.edu/~goldin>>

Oh, and I forgot to mention that the behavior is what
you expect (so far I've only looked at the Beetles model
as we're still trying to debug it).  When the step size
varies by a large percentage, you start to see deeper
trees being generated by NUTS for the lower step sizes.

I've attached a plot of rejects vs. step size and
tree depth (log2 # leapfrog steps) vs. step size.

How should we draw these kinds of things?  The way I
did it should be filed as a counterexample.  Faceted
side by side are hard to interpret, but if I could stack
them vertically it'd look OK -- I find ggplot2 really
hard to control even though I've read the book and get
the basic patterns.

NUTS tuning is pretty impressive.  67% accept rate.
And the accept rate's higher for lower step sizes.
And you see a very clear relationship between step size
and number of steps.

This geometry stuff really seems to work!

Stan is really fast now!  0.2s w. clang++ -O0
for 2000 iterations with data read, output write,
and adaptation.  I don't have the patience for a
g++ -O3 run (it's not so much the model as the libs,
which take forever to compile on my notebook).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 7/2/12 10:10 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
 > instead of saving 1/0 accept/reject, we
 > should be saving Pr(accept) at each step.
 > This contains slightly more information.

For what I reported, I just used the Coda trick of
checking if the parameters were the same iteration
to iteration -- I haven't saved anything yet.

For HMC, there's a straightforward Metropolis step
based on the new probability.

In NUTS, it's not so clear what I should report.

First, there's a slice variable u, which is sampled
between 0 and the current probability uniformly (if you
look at the code, it's all done on the log scale; Radford
discusses this in his paper with analysis of probability [aka
energy] change).

Then, points in the NUTS tree generated by leapfrog
steps are rejected if their probability is below the
slice variable.  The only way we get a full rejection is
if every leapfrog step produces parameters with probability
below the slice variable.   I suppose something like the max
of those might be a good proxy.

Overall, Matt's code's surprisingly easy to read.
If you're looking at the code, there's a very clever online
test to update the point that will be the next sample each
tree expansion step.  It's an instance of a general trick
to generate a random element from an array presented one
element at a time that you can't buffer.

- Bob

>     could leave boost and eigen out so the package is small.

> That is okay for now. I would recommend that RStan exclude eigen/ but have an explicit dependency on the RcppEigen
> package, now that they have overcome their PowerPC problems. The user would have to install Boost separately, but that
> is probably going to be in a default location like /usr/include/ or whatever is the Windows equivalent.

Stan only needs the headers from Eigen to compile user
models.

RcppEigen will need the Eigen headers, too, so
we could get the path from RcppEigen.

I'd very much like users like me to be able to configure
their own library include path if we're not going to
distribute Boost and Eigen with RStan.  I think it's also
a good idea to do this to have an alternative strategy
that's guaranteed to work no matter what happens to
third-party tools like RcppEigen.

I'm also still worried about version compatibility.  The
combinatorics of testing, much less supporting
multiple versions of Stan versus multiple versions
of Eigen/Boost are pretty daunting.

Life will be much simpler on the testing and maintenance
side if we only support the latest Stan w. the versions
of Eigen and Boost that go with it.

- Bob

On Tuesday, July 3, 2012 7:30:34 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'd very much like users like me to be able to configure

> distribute Boost and Eigen with RStan.  I think it's also
> a good idea to do this to have an alternative strategy
> that's guaranteed to work no matter what happens to
> third-party tools like RcppEigen.

This is not hard to do, although only a small minority will know how. At

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Using-Makevars

it says that the useR needs a Makevars file in the build directory or in $HOME/.R/ that defines PKG_CPPFLAGS with the relevant include paths, which will come before any include paths defined by RStan (when building from source).

That said, almost everybody on Windows and Mac will expect

install.packages("RStan")

to Just Work, and to do that we have to adhere to the CRAN guidelines on package size and whatnot so that they distribute RStan binaries for Windows and Mac.

> I'm also still worried about version compatibility.  The
> combinatorics of testing, much less supporting
> multiple versions of Stan versus multiple versions
> of Eigen/Boost are pretty daunting.

I think Eigen will be okay, but Boost might be more of an issue because there is a small chance that whatever is on CRAN is too old and whatever is on the Boost website might be too new someday. RcppEigen is presumably going to be "latest released Eigen", although it actually has had eigen 3.1-alpha for a while. For some reason, RcppEigen doesn't include FFT among its unsupported modules, so we should ask Doug to include FFT in the next RcppEigen upload, or we will have to include FFT ourselves in RStan.

Ben

> I doubt you want to put a dependency on Stan into
> mcmcplots.  Can't we just do all the glue stuff on

The way mcmcplots grew up was to working from coda::mcmc.list objects.
This data structure contains a list of coda::mcmc objects, each
representing one chain. (See ?coda::mcmc.list and ?coda::mcmc.) Each
chain contains all the posterior draws associated with each parameter.
It has no information on which draws are warm-up vs. post-warm-up, or
information on acceptance / rejection, or anything else at all. For
now, if RStan can feed mcmcplots this same data structure, then no
mcmcplots changes are required to work with RStan, but then mcmcplots
also could not display some of the visualizations that you'd like,
such as warm-up highlighting.

(By the way, on warm-up: JAGS does not return draws from its
adaptation phase at all. Is this a design decision with Stan to return
such draws?)

Opinion, your thoughts welcome: Long-term, my gut says to refactor
mcmcplots to use various accessor methods rather than manipulating the
data structure directly. This would remove the dependency on the
specific data format. RStan would have implementations for the
accessor methods for the Stan object. This would mean a contract
rather than a direct dependency between mcmcplots and RStan. Given the
widespread legacy use of the mcmc.list and mcmc objects, mcmcplots
would include implementations of the accessor methods for such
objects.

> Not every plot we do in RStan has to come from mcmcplots.
> But if you can add more diagnostic plots w/o dependencies on Stan,
> I'd say it's a good idea.

I'd say mcmcplots should contain whatever is widely applicable to MCMC
visualization.

> Often we want to scatterplot two parameters anyway to see what
> their covariance looks like.

That seems feasible, but what makes this special for MCMC vs a regular
R scatterplot?

> CMU (which is where computational linguistics lived before
> it moved 100% into comp sci).  I know Justine, of course.

And I used to work under David Evans at his spin-off. Small world.

Best,
Ilya

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] mcmcplots
messages.body_plain:
Here's why trace plots are special and are worth hardcoding (rather than just leaving the user to draw in R):
1.  If there is slow convergence, trace plots are a natural first place to look for diagnostics.  (If R.hat is fine, I don't bother looking at trace plots, but when there are problems, I like to go first to the trace plots).
2.  Traceplots use the parallel structure of the simulations--one color per chain.  That's specific to iterative simulations.  In contrast, scatterplots are simple and don't involve anything special with the chains (although I suppose we could make scatterplots showing a different color for each chain; if we wanted that, I'd support a special function such as mcmc.scatterplot to do this).

> Wow, this just seems like such overkill!  L=200 and then 10,000 iterations, for a problem that Gibbs does in 100 (or maybe 5000 in the standard parameterization without parameter expansion).  Really, though, the parameter expansion is key.  Straight Metrop without PX would get stuck forever if it started near tau=0.
This is basic HMC.  NUTS, with a diagonal mass
matrix, averages about 5 leapfrog steps per iteration.

We're starting with log(tau) = 0, so tau = 1.

I just ran lots of iterations because they're fast
(100K iterations is around 2s, so 10K was so fast
I didn't have to think about doing fewer).  It seems
to converge much faster.

The epsilon needs to be set for the lowest scale
and then the number of steps increased to avoid
a slow random walk in the slowest moving parameter.

- Bob

I agree that patents are even more innovation-stifling

to claims nobody cares about, like which DB and settings you
use.)

the GPL (and even more the AGPL) is to prevent freeloading

around it.  The copyleft makes them contribute back to the
community.  AGPL just extends GPL to software servers, right?

than BSD?

use my code, so I prefer BSD.

license.  That was to explicitly stop companies using the
code without paying us.  Companies pretty much all treat
GPL software libraries as poisonous (though they're happy to
use systems like MySQL and Linux).  Many of them treat any
open-source as poisonous because of copyright and patent
infringement issues (we've been advised that having our code
as open as it is opens the way to patent and copyright
litigtation that wouldn't be so easy if not everyone could
look at our code).

IANAL, nor have I ever been involved in a legal dispute over software, but I think that is basically right. AGPL adds 1 clause to the GPL 3 that roughly says if a server uses modified AGPL code to provide a service, it is distributing a derived work. That is why I think AGPL > GPL, but whether *GPL > BSD is a different debate.

And I think it is fair to say that a primary original motivation for *GPL licenses was to prevent people from distributing derived works without contributing the code back. That is still a big motivation, but nowdays there are other important considerations like patents, signing keys, etc. that are addressed by the FSF's licenses.

> As an academic, I just want as many people as possible to
> use my code, so I prefer BSD.

I'm in the same boat. But everything depends on what "use" means in practice. To me, if a license says, "you are free to use / modify / etc. this software but whoever might hold the tenuous patents is free to sue your ass for triple damages due to deliberate infringement", then the software isn't really free to use / modify / etc.

I think (and I think the FSF thinks) that GPL3 code developed under federal grants is largely immune from the worst patent-related scenarios. My argument is

1) The Bayl-Dole Act ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayh%E2%80%93Dole_Act ) requires the feds to be given a royalty-free license
2) Section 11 of the GPL3 precludes discriminatory patent deals
3) Thus, everybody is entitled to the same royalty-free patent deal that was given to the feds

But as far as I know, that hasn't been tested in a US court yet. If correct, then there is a tradeoff in that (A)GPL makes it harder for patent trolls but BSD makes it easier for real companies to use the code.

I dug a bit deeper into the linking issue, and
it's yet another legal grey area:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNU_General_Public_License#Linking_and_derived_works

The FSF apparently says that if you dynamically link to
GPL code and are not GPL, you're violating the GPL.
And R packages definitely get dynamically linked to R!

violating the GPL by trying to ACM-license an R package.

Anyway, I think we're OK if we:

1.  BSD-license Stan

2.  GPL-license RStan

The GPL contains a clause allowing GPL-ed code to link both
BSD and GPL code (which is what RStan does) without forcing
the linked BSD code to become GPL-ed itself.

>     What I've seen w.r.t. (1) is that people who get grants charge
>     the feds for "research" and claim that the "software" is developed
>     under their own nickel.  At least that's how everybody plays the
>     DARPA-funding game.
>
>
> Seems shady but maybe that is consistent with their grants.

Of course it's shady.  It's getting around the intent of the
funders.  But the grant language (we've only dealt with NIH
and DARPA and some smaller defense groups) only says that what
you do with money from the grant needs to be licensed to the
government.

>
>     I don't follow your point (2).  Just because I GPL something
>     can't mean I can use other people's patented technology.
>
>
> Right. So, if someone claims to have a patent on calculating a
> derivative, they could certainly troll Columbia for supporting Stan.
> What my 1, 2, 3 was intended to suggest was that Columbia would not
> have an economically viable way to file a bunch of patents on code
> that was GPL3 and then try to cash in on those patents with licenses
> or by selling the patent rights to patent trolls. Columbia could file
> patents, but the GPL3  wouldn't allow Columbia to license them for
> more than what it licenses them to the feds ($0.00). Thus, no patent
> troll would want to buy the patents from Columbia.

Aha -- thanks for the explanation.

>
>     We've found that every large company who bought software from our
>     company has insisted on indemnification vs. patents.  I've found this
>     ridiculuous, because if Oracle sues Comcast over their use of our
>     software, it's not like our little two-person company will be able
>     to do anything other than go bankrupt in response.   But that's how
>     the lawyers insist on structuring the deal, so every deal for us is
>     like a time bomb.
>
>     Patent trolls might sue Columbia, but they're not going to sue
>     you and me -- we don't (well, maybe I should only speak for myself)
>     have enough money to make it worthwhile.
>
>
> Maybe, but I wouldn't want to put anyone else in hot water over code I
> wrote if I can help it.
>

I agree.  But if you read patents, people have patents on
things like statistical sampling.  How can you avoid the risk?

I believe patents can be announced after you've already built code
that violates them.  I believe that's part of the usual patent troll
arsenal of tricks.  Suppose two inventors, A and B, generate the same
idea at the same time.  Both keep it to themselves, and both build
products based on the idea.  If A patents it and B hasn't published
the idea publicly, then A can sue B, even though B generated the
idea completely independently.  I think there might be some recourse
for B if they kept detailed records of their own invention -- I know
Bell Labs was fanatical (in theory -- in practice it was chaos) about
keeping hardback dated lab notebooks.  Some researchers even had the
habit of having other people sign their lab notebooks for corroboration
as to when they had the idea.

- Bob

messages.subject: piecewise (0,inf) -> (-inf,inf) transform?
messages.body_plain:
As is, when a variable is declared in Stan with
range (0,inf), a log transform is applied to unconstrain
it.  In practice, this means we inverse transform it using
the exponential function.  This is costly computationally.

Instead, we could use a transform f : (0,inf) -> (-inf,inf)
for some lower bound epsilon > 0 with

   f(x) = log x + (1 - log epsilon)  if x < epsilon, and

        = x / epsilon                if x >= epsilon.

Then the inverse function g : (-inf,inf) -> (0,inf) would be

   g(y) = exp(y) - (espilon - log epsilon)    if y < log epsilon, and

        = epsilon * y                         if y >= log epsilon.

The function g(y) is continuous and differentiable everywhere with

   g'(y) = exp(y)    if y < log epsilon

         = epsilon   if y >= log epsilon

leading to log Jacobian

   log | g'(y) | = y              if y < log epsilon, and

                 = log epsilon    if y >= log epsilon.

This will lead to faster transforms and fewer derivative terms
on the auto-dif stack.  It also prevents overflow as y -> inf.

I'm not clear on whether this will be a good or bad thing
geometry-wise for HMC.

- Bob

Finally, I managed to build rstan.so and libstan.so using -Os -s by adding a Makefile in src though Makefile is not encouraged due to it might be less portable.

It is not trivial to have a package defined CXXFLAGS (and other flags) as what is essentially done in R is

make -f 'Makevars' -f '/usr/lib/R/etc/Makeconf' -f '/usr/share/R/share/make/shlib.mk <http://shlib.mk>' -f '/home/jq/.R/Makevars' SHLIB_LDFLAGS='$(SHLIB_CXXLDFLAGS)' SHLIB_LD='$(SHLIB_CXXLD)' SHLIB='rstan.so'

The first Makevars is the package supplied src/Makevars.  So whatever I do regarding CXXFLAGS in src/Makevars would be overridden later.

But for src/Makefile, R does

make -f '/usr/lib/R/etc/Makeconf' -f 'Makefile' -f '/home/jq/.R/Makevars'

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] piecewise (0,inf) -> (-inf,inf) transform?
messages.body_plain:
I've played a fair number of games with these kinds of transforms and I've never found a satisfactory alternative to exp/log transforms.  The problem in your transform, for example, is that, while the transform and its first derivative are continuous, its second derivative (and hence in some sense the optimal step size) is not.  I'll have to take the opportunity to advocate for bouncing again -- it removes the need for the expensive transform and does not introduce any new Jacobians.

-Mike

On Jul 8, 2012, at 4:07 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> As is, when a variable is declared in Stan with
> range (0,inf), a log transform is applied to unconstrain
> it.  In practice, this means we inverse transform it using
> the exponential function.  This is costly computationally.
>
> Instead, we could use a transform f : (0,inf) -> (-inf,inf)
> for some lower bound epsilon > 0 with
>
>  f(x) = log x + (1 - log epsilon)  if x < epsilon, and
>
>       = x / epsilon                if x >= epsilon.
>
> Then the inverse function g : (-inf,inf) -> (0,inf) would be
>
>  g(y) = exp(y) - (espilon - log epsilon)    if y < log epsilon, and
>
>       = epsilon * y                         if y >= log epsilon.
>
> The function g(y) is continuous and differentiable everywhere with
>
>  g'(y) = exp(y)    if y < log epsilon
>
>        = epsilon   if y >= log epsilon
>
> leading to log Jacobian
>
>  log | g'(y) | = y              if y < log epsilon, and
>
>                = log epsilon    if y >= log epsilon.
>
> This will lead to faster transforms and fewer derivative terms
> on the auto-dif stack.  It also prevents overflow as y -> inf.
>
> I'm not clear on whether this will be a good or bad thing
> geometry-wise for HMC.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: diagnostic design
messages.body_plain:
I've been toying around with some design ideas for the diagnostic
plot. Here's a version that incorporates an Rhat display; it
essentially combines information from the left and right sides of the
R2WinBUGS figure that Andrew pointed out. Any comments?

This is a diagnostic plot, not a comprehensive display. For a vector
parameter like theta (say, theta[1]..theta[100]), we may not be able
to show estimates for each cell in the array. (Is vector the right
word?) My intuition is to always show caterpillars / Rhats for all
cells (up to the maximum that fits on the screen) that have Rhat
problems. If there's room, we would also randomly choose additional
cells.

Because it's an on-screen plot (you wouldn't include it in an academic
paper), I think use of color is fine.

One design choice here is that Rhats for all parameters would not be
grouped together in this kind of display (theta gets its own group of
Rhats, lambda underneath would get its own group, etc.)

Also, do we need to display the multivariate PSRF or no? Is that on
the same scale as univariate Rhat?

Best,
Ilya

-- Ilya Goldin <www.pitt.edu/~goldin <http://www.pitt.edu/~goldin>>

the overall Stan logo because:

add helicopers, jets, jetpacks, and wormhole spaceships
later.  We could even scale down to tricycles for a beginners
edition.

Or we could use both, with a tagline like:

    Transfer from the Gibbs Local to the Hamiltonian
    Express.

or

in the noise like a race car or an EU-funded presentation's
acknowledgements page.

but I think I can align right near any group of text in the
right-hand column.

those are more generic.

Today's legal topic:  trademark infringement.

to do this kind of stuff.  For instance, here's an academic
site that worked with a good designer:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] fma() and errors
messages.body_plain:
I thought about this a bit more and realized
that we'd been talking about being able to
just turn all the error checking on and off.
In that situation, we might want to add error
checking to everything.

Also, I think we can cut down on the implementations
with templates.  The top-level fma() function with
policy defaults can be handled just as for the normal
log density function.  This also saves having to generate
new items on the stack, which we definitely don't want
to do with these kinds of low-level functions.

Daniel and I can sort this out in a way that should
be transparent from the outside.

Also, we haven't decided how to remove bounds, overflow, and
domain checking.  Should we add our own property or use
NDEBUG?  I don't know much about how C++ projects get built
at this level of detail.

messages.subject: model error checking for undefined transformed params
messages.subject_clean: model error checking for undefined transformed params
messages.body_plain:
Daniel was running into segfaults from models with
undefined transformed params.  It's a programming error,
but we want to trap it and dump out an informative warning
message, not segfault!

So I added a test to the generated model code.
Every log-prob-gradient eval, it checks each
transformed parameter to make sure it was defined.  If not,
it throws an exception, which halts the model and reports
what went wrong.

An alternative would be to initialize then and initialize
to NaN or 0 or something.  But it seemed better to flag it.
Otherwise, the variables go through and have 0 variance in
the output and so mess up our convergence monitoring.

The model tests behave in a way I didn't expect if this
kind of exception crops up.  Daniel -- try declaring, but
not definining a transformed parameter and see what happens.

I added a method is_undefined() to stan::agrad::var
along with a test.  It'll succeed if you do something
like this:

    var x;
    x.is_uninitialized(); // evaluates to true
    x = 5;
    x.is_unitialized(); // evaluates to false

I also made sure to initialize a var's vi_ variable
to static_cast<vari*>(0) in the nullary constructor.

- Bob

On 7/14/12 4:26 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> You might be able to redefine the [] operator via the plugin mechanism if you feel that strongly about it, but I would
> say just don't use it.

I agree it's best not to use it, primarily to (a) be clear on
what's Eigen and what's std::vector, and (b) to prevent
ever using operator()[int] on a matrix by mistake (as in
that last bug).

 From what I can tell from the doc:

   http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/QuickRefPage.html

operator[](int) is just a synonym for operator()(int).  Both
do range checking unless NDEBUG nor EIGEN_NO_DEBUG is defined.

I suspect you'd get a duplicate operator definition if you
tried to inject operator[](int) using their plugin include.

There are probably still places in the code where
I do use operator[](int).  It simplifies some of the
code by letting me template out std and Eigen vectors

    std::vector<double>,
    Eigen::Matrix<double,Dynamic,1>, and
    Eigen::Matrix<double,1,Dynamic>.

The problem, of course, is Eigen::Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>,
which really must be accessed with either row(i) or (i,j).

- Bob

messages.subject: pushed 1-file R/Stan interface a la R2WinBUGS
messages.subject_clean: pushed 1-file R/Stan interface a la R2WinBUGS
messages.body_plain:
I pushed a very crude system-call-based R interface
to Stan in the form of a single file of function definitions
at the top level of the Stan release (I didn't want to mess up
Jiqiang's work on rstan):

    r2stan_sys.R

(No -- we're not going to call anything r2stan, but I
couldn't think of what else to call it without confusing
it with the existing rstan.)

Its interface follows R2WinBUGS, and it returns
an R2WinBUGS "bugs object" (which can be printed,
attached, plotted, and the variables returned with
structure or converted into a Coda object).

It requires that Stan be installed (which in turn
requires a modern-ish C++ compiler and make to be installed),
and the bin/stanc parser and bin/libstan library be pre-built.
This is all documented in gory detail in the appendix and
getting started sections of our reference manual.

Like R2WinBUGS, it uses system calls to invoke Stan.

The drawbacks compared to the deeper integration Jiqiang's
undertaking is that file I/O vs. C++/R integration is slow,
especially with lots of processes (cores) running.  The
use of R for storing the samples means more memory use.
It also means writing all the functionality to analyze
samples/chains in R.

The advantage is that Stan is completely independent of R
(and of Rcpp) when run this way -- we won't depend on their compilers,
their compiler options, versions of Boost, Eigen, etc.  It also means
we won't crash the R session if Stan segfaults (tries to read memory
it shouldn't).

Another bonus is that using R to store the samples means they'll
save and restore easily.  Also, piggybacking on R2WinBUGS
means instant Coda compatibility.

The ability to pull out just the named samples means
it'll be easy for Ilya to work on right away without
any direct dependency on Stan.

I think we'll be able to use some of the parallel
options in R to run chains on multiple cores pretty easily
(mclapply, in particular, looks promising).  To do this
from R directly in rstan depends on our finding some cross-platform
threading option (maybe Boost).

The current version won't work on Windows -- the file
naming convention and names of executables need to
be finessed.

Here's the declaration of the main function
(there are also some support functions to do things
like write data or inits files once).

stan = function(model.file,
                 cpp.file = "anon_model.cpp",
                 model.executable = "./a.out",
                 samples.dir = "samples",
                 data = NULL,
                 inits = NULL,
                 chains = 3,
                 seed = floor(runif(1,0,100000000)),
                 iter = 2000,
                 warmup = iter / 2,
                 thin = max(1, floor((iter - warmup) / 1000)),
                 leapfrog_steps = -1,
                 max_treedepth = 10,
                 epsilon = -1,
                 epsilon_pm = 0,
                 unit_mass_matrix = FALSE,
                 delta = 0.5,
                 gamma = 0.05,
                 test_grad = FALSE,
                 cc = "g++ -O3",
                 stan.home = STAN_HOME) {

It requires stan.home be set in order to be able to find Stan and lets
you control the compiler using cc (it must be compatible with
whatever was used to make Stan).  The other params should be familiar
from R2WinBUGS or from the Stan compiled model command doc.

I apologize in advance for the insanely clumsy R code.  I'm sure
many of my loops would be one-liners for the pros.

I also need to think about how to add make-like functionality
so as not to have to recompile each go round.  I had that in place,
but it wasn't making me happy when I changed models but stuck
with default intermediate file names.

Here's an example call to run the BUGS volume 1 example Rats
using their inits.  This example takes the silly
step of reading the data into the top-level R environment from
a file and then creating a list, which it then writes to
a file to send to Stan -- you could just send the file in
directly, but I wanted to show that it also worked like
R2WinBUGS.

messages.subject: Re: 8schools!?!?!?!? + epsilon/mass + epsilon*L = 1
messages.body_plain:
On 7/19/12 2:44 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> B
>
> I'll try some sims and see what happens.  I am happy to have separate mass matrix and epsilon.
 > I actually find it helpful to separate these.  As Mike explained to me, we can roughly think of the
 > mass matrix as corresponding to the variance of the target distribution (that's not really right
> in general but it makes sense in the simple case) and then it makes sense to have epsilon*L
> to be approx 1.

Just the separate mass matrix and epsilon are not
identified.  So you can always reascale epsilon
and the mass matrix so that epsilon * L = 1 if you're
doing HMC.  For NUTS, L isn't fixed, plus you sample
along the path, not just at the end.

I'd like to know what's special about 1 here.  NUTS II tries
to find an epsilon that works best for ALL params in terms
of achieving a 65% accept rate, then it fits a diagonal
mass matrix around that.  So I don't see why you'd wind
up with epsilon * L = 1 as a result.

My understanding is that if epsilon * L = 1, the
exact balance between epsilon and L involves
balancing so that L is small and epsilon is large for
efficient movement with epsilon being small enough for
accurate Hamiltonian simulation.

 > That's what you're getting:  you have epsilon*L as about 6, which isn't
 > far from the scale of most of the parameters in the model.
>
> Regarding the point at the end of your email, I'd be even happier if, instead of restarting a chain, we continued it at its current value with better tuning parameters.  If that doesn't work, we can restart.  But changing tuning parameters without changing the position would be cleaner.

We would be, too.  We only do this when we
can't continue the current value because it's NaN or
+/- infinity.  Once that's happen, there's no way to
get out of the hole through addition and multiplication.

I suppose we could go back to the initial values
and try again instead of regenerating those, too, but
often the problem is a poor (very low probability,
highly curved space) choice of starting point.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> Just the separate mass matrix and epsilon are not
> identified.  So you can always reascale epsilon
> and the mass matrix so that epsilon * L = 1 if you're
> doing HMC.  For NUTS, L isn't fixed, plus you sample
> along the path, not just at the end.

I would argue that the step size and the mass matrix are NOT
non-identified, even in regular HMC.  In the limit \epilson -> 0 that
might be true, but when \epsilon is non-zero you have to worry about
the momenta update,
a la p += -\epsilon * gradV (notice the mass matrix doesn't show up
here).  If \epsilon is too large then the update can be unstable, and
there's no mass matrix small enough to suppress that instability (you
know, other than zero).

(Matt and I have discussed this before.  He's in Bob's camp, but I'm
pretty sure the finite step size case is not the same as the ideal
case).

> I'd like to know what's special about 1 here.  NUTS II tries
> to find an epsilon that works best for ALL params in terms
> of achieving a 65% accept rate, then it fits a diagonal
> mass matrix around that.  So I don't see why you'd wind
> up with epsilon * L = 1 as a result.

If you've successfully standardized your distribution then it should
look like a standardized gaussian, where the width of the typical set
is about 1.  In that case the optimal distance to travel is 1 =
\epsilon * L.

I didn't even know there were camps!  I thought
this was just algebra.  But now that I re-read
section 5.4.2.4 in Radford's handbook paper,
where he concludes they're equivalent,
I see that he modifies the epsilons on the
p updates so that they are parameter dependent:

   p[i] += - epsilon[i] * gradV[i]

He then concludes that the resulting position/momentum
values "can no longer be interpreted as following Hamiltonian
dynamics at consistent time points" and goes on to
say "but that is of no consequence for the use of these
trajectories in HMC".

 From the above, Michael's talking about the natural
mass-based physical update, which takes

   p[i] += epsilon * gradV[i]

I'm guessing Matt was talking about Radford's, so you
were considering different definitions of varying step
size.

Now I'll have to dive into our code to see what NUTS is
actually doing, having not recognized this distinction earlier.

> If you've successfully standardized your distribution then it should
> look like a standardized gaussian, where the width of the typical set
> is about 1.  In that case the optimal distance to travel is 1 =
> \epsilon * L.

But isn't epsilon * L equal to time, not distance traveled?
With fixed epsilon and L, distance traveled has to depend  on
the initial position and initial random momentum.

- Bob

Extreme mass matrices lead to large momenta which must be suppressed by the multiplication by the mass matrix upon the position updates. If we had infinite precision computers then the two approaches would give the same results, but on finite precision machines you can encounter adding/subtracting large numbers. I think the bigger issue, however, is that the large momenta updates can pass the stability threshold and cause the trajectory to diverge.

The mathematical question is whether or not the stability threshold scales with the mass matrix or not.  That's probably a better definition of our camps.  :-)

> But isn't epsilon * L equal to time, not distance traveled?
> With fixed epsilon and L, distance traveled has to depend  on
> the initial position and initial random momentum.

Ah, but remember that the average magnitude of the momentum is the square root of the dimension, which is order unity, and 1*1=1.  In RMHMC the idea is that the more complicated momenta distribution helps to compensate so that the total distance traveled is just right for any distribution.

messages.body_plain:
NUTS is using the Radford-style parameter-specific step sizes, which
produces discretized dynamics for the positions (and the energy of the
momenta) that are equivalent to using a diagonal mass matrix with
appropriate variances, which is equivalent to transforming the space
that the variables live in to (hopefully) look more like a standard
normal.

I am pretty much 100% confident that the overall scale of the inverse
mass matrix and the squared step size are completely interchangeable
in the sense that scaling the inverse mass matrix by c and the step
size by 1/sqrt(c) will produce no change in the discretized dynamics
of the position vector or the energy of the momentum vector. (The
momenta will be different, but they'll have the same energy.)

If I may be pedantic, the width of the typical set of a standard
normal is more like 4 or 6 than 1. To continue to be (slightly less)
pedantic, if you've really transformed things so that you're working
with a standard normal, then I'm not sure that you really want to
always travel for epsilon*L=size of typical set, since you may hit a
weird resonance.

Matt

produces discretized dynamics for the positions (and the energy of the
momenta) that are equivalent to using a diagonal mass matrix

P.S.  here's the silly function I wrote to compute split R-hat.  I don't have the new n_eff, though; I'm waiting on all of you to create that!

monitor.split <- function (a){
  dims <- dim(a)
  n <- dims[1]
  m <- dims[2]
  a1 <- a[1:(n/2),,]
  a2 <- a[(n/2+1):n,,]
  dims.fat <- c(n/2,2*m,dims[3])
  a.fat <- array (NA, dims.fat)
  dimnames (a.fat) <- dimnames(a)
  a.fat[,1:m,] <- a1
  a.fat[,(m+1):(2*m),] <- a2
  return (monitor (a.fat))
}

Matt

looked at the model.  The answer is that each term in the sum is constrained
to be negative because alpha and beta are constrained < 0 and the
xa and xs are all positive.

success param is outside of (0,1).

and the step size adapted to 4e+35!  Something's definitely
off in the model.  I'll take another side-by-side squint at it.

messages.subject: good news
messages.body_plain:
I got the 8 schools working (pretty much, if not perfect) by randomizing epsilon and L at each step.  Not to stop periodicity but to allow HMC to get stuck from places where big steps or long chains will invariably get rejected.  Currently I'm setting epsilon and L independent:
    epsilon <- runif (1, 0, 2*epsilon.0)
    L <- ceiling (2*L.0*runif(1))
But now I'm thinking it could be logical to have them be positively correlated.

> rejection.

What happens is that in the constrained parameter version (sigma unlogged, no bouncing), the chains go off to negative sigma -> rejection.
When I tried unlogged sigma _with_ bouncing, the chains, if they ever got near zero, would get ricocheted off to huge values of sigma -> rejection.  The problem arose because of huge gradients on sigma.
When I tried log sigma, the chains would again sometimes go to extreme values.

The only way to avoid rejection was with tiny step sizes, and then there was no mixing.

> the total gradient would push away from 0 unless the

Yeah, it sounds like there's not enough data to temper the prior and you're essentially trying to sample from 1/\sigma.

What isn't clear to me is why you're getting such extreme ricochets.  As you approach zero from positive values the gradients increase, which increases the momenta.  When you finally bounce, then, the reflected momenta will be large.  But as you continue back through positive values the gradients should temper that momentum -- modulo the small epsilon you move past the origin the evolution should be symmetric with p -> -p.  So unless you started at huge values of sigma I'm not sure how you're able to bounce to them.

Have you checked that the magnitude of the momenta along sigma is equal before and after the bounce?

> bounce?  I'd have thought that as sigma approaches 0,
> the total gradient would push away from 0 unless the
> coefficients were all very tightly clustered.

What happens is that when sigma is near zero, d(log p)/d(sigma) gets huge.  Without bouncing, this sends HMC off to big negative values and rejection.  With bouncing, it sends HMC off to big positive values.  The problem is the persistence of the momentum variable.  It goes like this:  sigma is 0.6, say, and then the gradient is huge, then the momentum is huge, then it gets bounced off to sigma = 50 or so, now the gradient is negative but small, so it takes a long long long time for the momentum to get back negative.  In the meantime, sigma becomes more and more extreme.

> mixing that was good enough to satisfy R-hat on multiple
> chains from diffuse starting points.
>

Yes, I got that too (with log sigma) but then I was getting 99-100% accept rates, which didn't make me so happy.  I preferred the results with random epsilon and L at each step.

hmc.iteration <- function (th, y, s.y, L, epsilon, M){
  d <- length (th)
  phi <- rnorm (d, 0, 1)
  th.old <- th
  log.p.old <- log.p.th <http://log.p.th> (th,y,s.y) - 0.5*sum(phi^2)
  phi <- phi + 0.5*epsilon*gradient.th <http://gradient.th> (th, y, s.y)
  for (l in 1:L){
    th <- th + epsilon*phi
    if (th[10] < 0) {
      th[10] <- - th[10]
      phi[10] <- - phi[10]
    }
    phi <- phi + (if (l==L) 0.5 else 1)*epsilon*gradient.th <http://gradient.th> (th, y, s.y)
  }
  phi <- -phi
  log.p.star <- log.p.th <http://log.p.th> (th,y,s.y) - 0.5*sum(phi^2)
  r <- exp (log.p.star - log.p.old)
  if (is.nan(r)) r <- 0
  p.jump <- min(r,1)
  th.new <http://th.new> <- if (runif(1) < p.jump) th else th.old
  return (list (th=th.new <http://th.new>, p.jump=p.jump))

}

On Jul 23, 2012, at 3:26 PM, McLaughlin, Michael P. wrote:

> Hello,
>
> Thank you very much for your response.  It was pretty much what I expected and I've been working along those lines but not sure of success, yet.
>
> I had never heard of Stan before and I glanced over the documentation a bit.  [Don't know if I can squeeze in another learning curve right now, however.]
>
> One comment.  [Perhaps you've already tried this.]  In Xcode (which I use all the time), it should be possible to create a single project for any model with the Stan compilation as a (constant) dependent project.  That way, following your documentation, anon_model.cpp could be generated first then the final executable (a.out or equivalent) second, all with one keystroke (Command-B).  If you wanted to do more, Xcode supports parallelization via the Accelerate framework, esp. nice for HMC.  You would also have the benefit of a symbolic debugger (e.g., LLDB).
>
> --
> Michael P. McLaughlin
>
> From: Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu>
> Date: Saturday, July 21, 2012 3:46 PM
> To: Michael McLaughlin <mp...@mitre.org>
> Subject: Re: Real data can be a pain
>
> Hi--I think this should work fine in Stan (or any other Bayesian software) if you just model the steps 1, 2, 3 directly:
>
> For step 1, you have your mixture model.  You just need to put an informative prior distribution on the parameters of the mixture components to get a stable estimate.
>
> For step 2, just model the quantization:  if the data from step 1 are z_i, and the rounded data are y_i, then set up a model for y|z, maybe just a simple rounding model.  The z's are now missing data.  Or in this case (a mixture of normal and laplace densities for z), you should be able to simply integrate out the missingness to get a probability distribution for the rounded data, z.
>
> For step 3, I don't quite know what you mean by "interpolated to an unobserved location."  Again, though, this is just some process that can be modeled.
>
> The moral of the story is:  likelihood inference really works!  The trick is to model the data and then do the inference, rather than trying to jump directly to create an estimate from the data.
>
> A
>
> On Jul 19, 2012, at 8:48 PM, McLaughlin, Michael P. wrote:
>
> > Dear Prof. Gelman,
> >
> > Thought this might be suitable for your blog.
> >
> > Some time ago, I was handed a dataset that needed to be modeled.  It was generated as follows:
> > Random navigation errors, historically a binary mixture of Normal and Laplace with a common mean, were collected by observation.
> > Sadly, these data were recorded with too few decimal places so that the resulting quantization is clearly visible in a scatterplot.
> > The quantized data were then interpolated (to an unobserved location).
> > The final result looks like fuzzy points (small scale jitter) at quantized intervals spanning a much larger scale (the parent mixture distribution).  This fuzziness, likely ~Normal or ~Laplace, results from the interpolation.  Otherwise, the data would look like a discrete analogue of the Normal/Laplace mixture.
> >
> > I would like to characterize the latent Normal/Laplace mixture distribution but the quantization is "getting in the way".  When I tried MCMC on this problem (using JAGS) and simply ignoring the quantization, it turned out that the "signal" coming from the jitter overwhelmed that due to the underlying parent mixture so that the MCMC process did not "see" the Normal/Laplace distribution very well.  That is, it returned unrealistic parameters for it, with values more in tune with the jitter than with the parent distribution.  In other words, it thought it was modeling the jitter.
> >
> > So I cannot ignore the quantization.  Unfortunately, I have not found any way to incorporate it into a valid MCMC model either.  I've searched everywhere I can find but have uncovered no examples for treating quantization error corrupting a parent distribution.
> >
> > Do you, or your readers, have any suggestions.
> >
> > Thanks very much.
> >
> > --
> > Michael P. McLaughlin
>

messages.subject: Stan and Xcode
messages.body_plain:
Michael:

Thanks for your hints at how to use Xcode, which Andrew
forwarded to our developer's list (and to which I'm also
replying).

We use a mix of Mac, Windows and Linux, but none of us
know Xcode (we just use it to get the command-line tools,
which we then use scripted through make or through R;  in
the intro, I wanted to actually explain the compile steps).

I'll give the GUI a whirl, and if it doesn't require
too much config, I'll add a note to the doc (with
thanks, of course).

 > these data were recorded with too few decimal
 > places so that the resulting quantization is clearly
 > visible in a scatterplot.

For modeling the quantization error you mention, one
thing you can do is introduce a latent true location
and model the quantization process (for instance by restricting
the true location to an interval that would quantize to the
value you observe).  That lets you jointly
infer the original data and use it inference.  This is
the strategy outlined in Andrew's book(s) for censored
data, but the idea's the same.

- Bob

messages.subject: Windows builds + makefiles (important for release)
messages.body_plain:
We can't really release until I finish the doc,
and I can't do that until I understand the builds.

I merrily went along documenting direct calls
to g++ from Unix in the first pass at the doc.

Now I have two problems:

1.  Targets (and ?) differ on Windows.  But I'm not sure
exactly how (Java beautifully encapsulated the distinctions
so I never had to worry about it).

I know there's a .exe involved somewhere and the paths
are different.

Do I also need to call make differently?

I'd like to indicate at least in a footnote
how Windows users might be able to use Stan!

Or should I just have a complete set of parallel
instructions?  I suppose judging from Andrew's experience
on the install, I should be as explicit as possible in
every possible place someone might go off the rails
due to uncertainty.

2.  We have introduced a pretty strong dependency
on make for building bin/stanc and bin/libstan.a.

So maybe I should give up all pretense of being able
to operate without make and just provide instructions
for building models based on make?

Daniel -- can you remind me what that looks like?  I
couldn't quite understand the output of "make help":

  - models/* : If a Stan model exists at src/models/*.stan, this target
                      will copy the Stan model to models/*.stan, then
build the
                      Stan model.
   - *        : If a Stan model exists at *.stan, this target will build
                      the Stan model as an executable.

Is there a way to build without copying the model and
all its data and then running from a different location?
Moving is OK for the tiny bugs models.  But what does hte
second - * do?

- Bob

messages.subject: really need Eigen-vectorized distributions
messages.body_plain:
I'm going to try to generalize what Matt did
for the normal with std::vector to Eigen vectors.
The reason is that I want to support data matrix *
coefficient vector multiplication.  (I'm in the middle
of writing the documentation for efficiency and
vectorization.)  Ben's been urging this all along,
but it's now totally motivated by the efficiency of
Marcus's speedups to the matrix auto-dif.

The code's very abstract, but not actually that
complex.  Although Eigen vectors and std::vector are
roughly compatible (both support size and both
support []), I plan to just wrap an Eigen vector in
a view the same way Matt wrapped std::vector.

Daniel vectorized a couple more distributions after
normal and found a bug that we fixed in the size
constraints (the right constraint is that all vectors
need to be the same size; the original just checked if
they were all length 1 or equal to the max length,
which Daniel's unit testing uncovered).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: HMCMC
messages.body_plain:
I'm familiar with Runge-Kutta methods (of which
the Euler method is a simple explicit instance)
because we use the leapfrog integrator in Stan.

The Euler method is described here:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_method

Given a simple diffeq w. initial value:

    y'(t) = f(t,y(t));    y(t0) = y0

The algorithm (in pseudocode that's close to what the
real code would look like is):

euler(function y,
       double y0,
       double epsilon) {

    yy[0] = y0;

    tt[0] = 0;

    for (n = 0; ; ++n) {

      tt[n+1] = tt[n] + h;

      yy[tt[n+1]] = yy[tt[n]] + epsilon * f(tt[n],yy[tt[n]]);

      if (???) return yy[tt[n+1]];  // what is stop condition?

    }
}

We can auto-dif the function Euler w.r.t. y0 or epsilon,
but I'm somehow guessing that you want the derivative of
something at the solution.  But I have no idea how this all
fits together as part of a statistical model or how you'd go
about differentiating w.r.t. the return value.

- Bob

all-in-one-command thing like R2WinBUGS.

You only do ESS calculations AFTER "running Stan".
If you run multiple chains in parallel,
you'll have multiple chains to put into ESS.

That's how I built the system-call R interface and
presumably what Jiqiang's doing in the real RStan.

- Bob

The last answer on this page http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1101545/problem-with-gprof-on-os-x-program-is-not-of-the-host-architecture
says gprof is not working on mac.  Instead, using Shark in Xcode.

I tried gprof on linux, which seems give me some results.  I could dig in more on this issue.

In addition, repost what I said about the effective sample size just to say that this has nothing to do with R.

To demonstrate that, I added a fake test as follows, which needs 131138ms to finish
on my computer.

TEST(McmcChains,effective_sample_size) {
  std::vector<std::string> names;
  std::vector<std::vector<size_t> > dimss;
  stan::mcmc::read_variables("src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools1.csv", 3,
                             names, dimss);

  stan::mcmc::chains<> c(4, names, dimss);
  add_chain(c, 0, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools1.csv", 3);
  add_chain(c, 1, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools2.csv", 3);
  add_chain(c, 2, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools2.csv", 3);
  add_chain(c, 3, "src/test/mcmc/test_csv_files/8schools2.csv", 3);

  size_t index = 0;
  EXPECT_NEAR(13.08, c.effective_sample_size(index), 0.01) <<
    "the first sample size should be 13.1";
}

--
Jiqiang

On 7/25/12 4:22 PM, Frederic Bois wrote:
> (bounced back because I cannot email stan-dev, resending:)
> OK.
> The stopping would be "if tt[n+1] >= final_time" (with simple
> provision not to over-shoot)
> Now, something is missing. We need to introduce parameters theta:
>    y'(t) = f(t,y(t), theta);    y(t0) = y0
>
> In the Bayesian numerical statistical inference problem you would aim
> at getting a sample
> of theta from their posterior, given a prior and data likelihood.
> Likelihood would be a
> function of y, and hence of theta (and possibly some more usual
> statistical parameters sigma...)
>
> So you would want the Jacobian of y w.r.t. theta at some points.
>
> There is no need to get the Jacobian of y' wrt y in that problem, only
> implicit (e.g. Gear's) integrators use that.
> My suggestion is just to use simple Euler (or RG) for getting Jac(y |
> theta), even if the actual integration is done with
> a more sophisticated (and stable) integrator (which might use Jac(y' |
> y), but that's a separate issue, even if synergistic in terms of
> computing speed is AD capability is available).
>
> FB

messages.subject: parallelization
messages.body_plain:
There are two options for parallelization.

The easier route is just to run in several processes,
each in a single thread.  The data gets copied for each
chain and there may be a bit of I/O contention depending
on the size of the output and buffering to disk.  This
would include using a cluster to run on several machines.

The harder route is to get serious about making
Stan run in multi-threaded mode.  The code's there now,
but it hasn't been tested cross platform and there's
not an easy way to turn multithreading on/off (with it
on, the autodif slows down by about 15% due to thread
contention for the thread-local auto-dif stacks.

- Bob
